scenario: AITA for telling my mother she is the reason I won't wear white to my wedding? | I'm engaged. Planning on a small semi-formal beach wedding. Mum tells me that she can't wait to go wedding dress shopping with me and she wants to book an appointment at this fancy bridal shop in town. I told mum that I didn't want a white dress and that shop did just white bridal dresses and nothing else (I'd already looked it up). I think the whole concept of white wedding dresses is stupid. It only started with Queen Vic so it's not some ancient tradition and the ship has sailed on the whole white = pure/innocent/virginal thing. However, the main and the defining reason I am anti white wedding dress, is that my mother wore a white dress when she got married, and she and dad are divorced now. Every other woman in my family has worn a coloured dress to get married in (usually either blue or red and either really pale or really dark, with not much in between) and they have all had long (mostly) happy marriages that were either til death did them part or are still going strong today. When mum asked why I didn't want a white dress I first gave the the Queen Vic line which mum said wasn't enough justification, and then the bit about how I'm not exactly "innocent", which was an awful conversation to have with my mother. When she said that wasn't good enough I said "because I just don't want a white dress and I think coloured dresses look nicer and it's my wedding so I get to pick my clothes". Mum asked a few more times what the real reason was and I eventually admitted that her being the only woman to break the tradition and also the only woman to get divorced didn't exactly instill me with confidence in white dresses. Mum got really quiet, then I saw she was crying. She said she tried her best and that I spoke to her like that when I know how the divorce upset her was really cruel. I haven't apologised yet but I feel like she backed me into a corner and wouldn't accept any of the 3 perfectly fine answers I'd given before that, and I shouldn't have had to justify myself to begin with as it is my wedding so the only people whose opinions matter are me and my fiance. I also feel like if she had just accepted my choice or any of the first 3 answers I gave then I would not be in this situation. AITA?

Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. The user is asking if they're "AITA" (Am I the Asshole) for telling their mother that she's the reason they won't wear white to their wedding. 

First, I need to understand the scenario fully. The person is engaged and planning a small, semi-formal beach wedding. Their mother wants to go wedding dress shopping together at a specific bridal shop that only does white dresses. The person doesn't want a white dress and has already looked up the shop, knowing it only does white dresses. They think the white wedding dress tradition is silly, starting with Queen Victoria, and that the symbolism of white as pure or innocent is outdated. 

The main reason they're against a white dress is that their mother wore white and got divorced. All other women in the family wore colored dresses and had long, mostly happy marriages. When the mother asked why they didn't want a white dress, the person first gave the Queen Victoria line, which the mother dismissed as insufficient. Then they mentioned not being "innocent," which led to an awkward conversation. When pressed further, the person admitted that their mother being the only one to break the tradition and get divorced made them lose confidence in white dresses. The mother got upset, cried, and said that the person spoke to her cruelly, knowing how the divorce had affected her. The person hasn't apologized yet and feels the mother backed them into a corner, making them justify their choice when it's their wedding and their choice.

Now, to evaluate if the action is morally acceptable. The action in question is the person telling their mother that her divorce is the reason they don't want a white dress. 

I need to consider the moral aspects here. On one hand, the person is making a personal choice about their wedding attire, and it's their right to choose what they feel comfortable in. They have valid reasons, both personal and traditional, for not wanting a white dress. However, the way they communicated their reasons, especially the part about their mother's divorce, could be seen as insensitive or hurtful. 

The mother was emotional and felt hurt, which indicates that the way the information was delivered was not considerate of her feelings. The person might have been justified in their choice, but the manner in which they expressed their reasons, particularly linking it to their mother's divorce, could be seen as cruel or unkind. 

Additionally, the person feels that the mother shouldn't have pressed them for the real reason, but in any relationship, especially parent-child, there's an expectation of honesty and openness. However, honesty doesn't always mean delivering information in a way that could cause emotional pain. 

So, while the person's choice is their own, the way they communicated their reasons, especially the part about the mother's divorce, might be considered morally unacceptable because it caused unnecessary emotional harm. It's important to balance personal choices with sensitivity towards others' feelings, especially in close relationships.
